Run a 5-participant first-impression rating using a semantic differential scale and compare results against brief criteria.

junior: Tools used: paper observation sheet, stopwatch, screen recording app (e.g. Loom), tally sheet for errors.

Analyse moderated session logs (n=5) for task-completion rate, error patterns, and SUS score, then form prioritised recommendations.

def.junior: Whether your outcome does the job it was designed to do — as described in your brief. It links directly to your specifications (what it must measure up to) and the original need (who it was designed for). In its broadest sense, fitness for purpose also asks: were the right processes used to make it? This includes checking whether resources were used sustainably, whether the people involved were treated fairly, whether testing was done ethically, and whether the outcome can be responsibly disposed of at the end of its life.
def.senior: The ability of a technological outcome to serve its intended purpose within its intended context, as defined by the brief. Fitness for purpose is demonstrated by evaluating the outcome against each specification and confirming the original need is met. In its broadest sense, the concept extends beyond the outcome itself to include the fitness of the practices used in its development — encompassing the sustainability of resources, ethical testing and trialling procedures, cultural appropriateness, treatment of people involved in manufacture, lifecycle analysis, and ultimate disposal. This broader framing locates fitness for purpose within the philosophical understanding of the Nature of Technology: the performance of an outcome is only one factor in a positive fitness-for-purpose judgement.

junior: Need: students with nut allergies need a safe, affordable canteen snack.
Specification: nut-free production facility, no fridge required, costs under $1.20, fresh for 2 weeks.
Fit for purpose (outcome): the bar passes all four specification checks AND the target group actually chooses to eat it.
Fit for purpose (broader — practice): ingredients were sourced ethically; taste-testing used informed consent; packaging is compostable; no food waste was sent to landfill during development.
senior: Need: students with coeliac disease require a canteen option produced in a certified gluten-free facility within the existing price range.
Specifications: ≤8 g sugar/30 g serve; nut-free certified facility; aW ≤0.85 (14-day ambient shelf life); cost ≤$1.20/unit at pilot scale.
Fit for purpose (outcome): all four specifications are met AND ≥70% consumption rate is achieved in the target group trial.

Fit for purpose (broader — practice): supply chain audited for fair labour conditions; trialling conducted with culturally appropriate consent processes; packaging lifecycle assessed for end-of-disposal pathway; development food waste composted.

junior: Need: students need a uniform that keeps them cool during summer sport.
Specification: fabric must wick sweat, not go see-through when wet, and survive the school wash cycle.
Fit for purpose (outcome): all three specification checks are passed AND wear-test students report feeling cooler than in the old uniform.
Fit for purpose (broader — practice): fabric was ethically sourced; student wear-testers gave informed consent; old uniform offcuts were recycled rather than landfilled.
senior: Need: hospital patients require garments allowing clinical access that can be laundered at 90 °C without deteriorating.
Specifications: MVTR ≥5000 g/m²/24hr; opacity ≥90% when wet; dimensional stability ≤2% after 50 washes at 90 °C; fastens one-handed.
Fit for purpose (outcome): all four specifications are verified AND patients report the garment maintains their dignity.

Fit for purpose (broader — practice): garment trialling followed hospital ethics protocols; fabric certified under OEKO-TEX Standard 100 (no harmful substances); end-of-life pathway identified (textile recycling programme); garment workers in supply chain paid living wage (verified via audit).

junior: Need: elderly people need a grab bar that is easy to install and strong enough to hold their weight safely.
Specification: must hold 150 kg, install without drilling tiles, and pass basic safety checks.
Fit for purpose (outcome): load test is passed AND an elderly person can install it themselves without help.

Fit for purpose (broader — practice): testing involved older adult participants who gave informed consent; materials are corrosion-resistant and recyclable at end of life; no hazardous finishes were used.
senior: Need: elderly residents require grab rails that can be surface-mounted without tile penetration and support 150 kg lateral static load.
Specifications: lateral static load ≥150 kg (AS 1428.1); no tile drilling required; tool-free installation in ≤15 min; corrosion-resistant finish.
Fit for purpose (outcome): all four specifications are met AND an older adult installs the rail unassisted in a timed trial.

Fit for purpose (broader — practice): trialling conducted with occupational therapist oversight and full participant consent; stainless steel specified for longevity and recyclability; adhesive system assessed for VOC emissions and safe removal; supply chain checked for fair labour practices.

junior: Need: new immigrants need signs they can understand without reading English.
Specification: must use icons and visuals, be readable at 5 m, and pass a colour contrast check.
Fit for purpose (outcome): all three specification checks are passed AND non-English-speaking users navigate correctly in a wayfinding test.

Fit for purpose (broader — practice): testing involved diverse language groups with informed consent; symbols were reviewed for cultural appropriateness; print materials used recycled stock and soy-based inks.
senior: Need: non-English-speaking transit users require wayfinding signage communicating route information independent of any single language.
Specifications: contrast ratio ≥4.5:1 (WCAG AA); legible at 5 m under standard lux; uses ISO 7010 symbols; ≥90% correct navigation by unfamiliar users in testing.
Fit for purpose (outcome): all four specifications are verified AND non-English-speaking participants navigate correctly without assistance.

Fit for purpose (broader — practice): user testing included culturally diverse participants recruited through community organisations; symbols reviewed by a cross-cultural design consultant; print production specified on FSC-certified stock; digital version optimised to reduce energy per page load.

junior: Need: visually impaired users need a checkout that works with a screen reader.
Specification: must load in under 2 seconds, work on iPhone and Android, and pass a basic accessibility check.
Fit for purpose (outcome): all three specification checks are passed AND a screen-reader user completes a purchase without help.

Fit for purpose (broader — practice): usability testing involved participants with lived experience of visual impairment; user data was handled in line with the Privacy Act; the app is hosted on a renewable-energy server.
senior: Need: visually impaired users require an e-commerce checkout fully operable via screen reader and keyboard-only navigation.
Specifications: FCP ≤1.8 s on 4G; iOS 15+ and Android 11+ compatible; WCAG 2.1 Level AA (zero critical axe violations); ≥90% task completion by first-time users in ≤3 min.
Fit for purpose (outcome): all four specifications are met AND a screen-reader user completes the full checkout path unassisted.

Fit for purpose (broader — practice): testing recruited participants with visual impairments via a disability advocacy organisation under full ethical consent; personal data anonymised and deleted post-trial (Privacy Act 2020); hosting specified on renewable-energy infrastructure; software dependencies audited for open-source licence compliance; product carbon footprint documented.

def.junior: A real problem or requirement that a person, group, or place has. A need is identified from an issue within a context — it describes what is missing or not working. Your technological outcome should attempt to meet this need.
def.senior: An identified requirement of a person, group, or environment. A need is identified from an issue and sits within a context. It is distinct from an opportunity in that it describes something that is lacking or inadequate, rather than a possibility to improve or extend. Technological practice can be undertaken in an attempt to meet an identified need.

junior: Issue: students with coeliac disease have no safe option at the school canteen.
Need: a gluten-free, affordable lunch option produced in a certified facility so those students can eat safely at school.
senior: Issue: students with coeliac disease are excluded from canteen purchasing due to cross-contamination risk.

Need: a canteen product produced in a certified gluten-free facility, meeting the Codex Alimentarius standard of ≤20 ppm gluten, priced within the existing canteen range — so these students have genuine, safe access to a hot or cold lunch.

junior: Issue: students are overheating and underperforming during summer PE because the current uniform fabric does not breathe.
Need: a sports uniform made from moisture-wicking fabric that keeps students cool enough to participate comfortably in summer sport.
senior: Issue: current sports uniform fabric has an MVTR below 2000 g/m²/24hr, causing thermal discomfort during summer PE, with student survey data showing 68% report reduced participation.

Need: a replacement garment in certified moisture-wicking fabric (MVTR ≥5000 g/m²/24hr) that maintains opacity and survives the school laundry cycle — enabling full student participation regardless of temperature.

junior: Issue: elderly residents in a rest home cannot safely use the bathroom without support, but grab bars require professional installation.
Need: a grab bar that is strong enough to prevent falls and can be installed independently by older adults without drilling into tiles.
senior: Issue: 43% of falls among rest-home residents occur in bathrooms; current commercial grab rails require tile-penetrating fixings that residents or family cannot install without a licensed tradesperson.

Need: a surface-mounted grab rail that supports ≥150 kg lateral static load (AS 1428.1), installs without tile penetration, and can be fitted by a non-tradesperson in under 15 minutes — reducing fall risk without dependence on scheduled maintenance.

junior: Issue: new immigrants are arriving at a library and cannot navigate the building because all signs are in English only.
Need: wayfinding signage that communicates location and direction clearly to people who do not read English.
senior: Issue: a central library serves a community in which 31% of users identify a language other than English as their primary language; current signage relies entirely on English text and is rated "confusing" by 72% of non-English-speaking survey respondents.

Need: a wayfinding system communicating route, location, and service information through standardised iconography (ISO 7010) and spatial logic — independent of any single language — so all users can navigate the building without assistance.

junior: Issue: visually impaired users cannot complete purchases on a popular online store because the checkout does not work with their screen reader.
Need: an accessible checkout that a visually impaired user can operate fully using a screen reader and keyboard alone.
senior: Issue: automated accessibility audit (axe DevTools) identifies 17 critical WCAG 2.1 failures in the checkout flow; moderated testing with screen-reader users records a 0% task-completion rate on the payment step.

Need: a fully WCAG 2.1 Level AA-compliant checkout, operable via NVDA/VoiceOver and keyboard-only navigation across all critical transaction paths, so visually impaired users can purchase independently.

junior: Plants need water while the classroom is empty.
senior: Use evidence of the actual watering problem to establish a need with the caretaker and teacher.

def.junior: A chance to make something new or better — identified from an issue within a context. An opportunity is different from a need: instead of something being broken or missing, there is a positive possibility to create, improve, or extend something. Technological practice can be undertaken to realise an identified opportunity.
def.senior: An identified possibility for a person, group, or environment. Like a need, an opportunity is identified from an issue and sits within a context — but it describes a positive opening to improve, extend, or create, rather than a deficit to fix. Technological practice can be undertaken to realise an identified opportunity.

junior: Issue: more students are choosing plant-based diets but the school canteen has no plant-based hot option.
Opportunity: to create a tasty, affordable plant-based lunch that gives these students a real choice at the canteen.
senior: Issue: canteen sales data shows a 34% increase in students identifying as plant-based or flexitarian over three years, yet zero plant-based hot options are currently offered.

Opportunity: to develop a protein-dense (≥15 g/serve), shelf-stable plant-based snack targeting post-training recovery, priced at ≤$1.50 retail — realising a clear market gap while improving nutritional equity.

junior: Issue: students are throwing away clothes with small holes or tears rather than repairing them.
Opportunity: to design a visible-mending kit that makes repairs look intentional and stylish, so students are motivated to fix clothes instead of discarding them.
senior: Issue: New Zealand households discard an estimated 32 kg of clothing per person annually; repair cafés report demand outstripping volunteer capacity, with 78% of attendees aged 18–35.

Opportunity: to develop a premium visible-mending patch kit that reframes garment damage as a design feature — tapping into slow-fashion values among a younger audience and reducing textile waste at the point of individual behaviour change.

junior: Issue: schools with 3D printers rarely use them to make things that directly help students with physical differences.
Opportunity: to use the school's 3D printer to design and produce custom equipment or adaptive tools for students who need them.
senior: Issue: FDM 3D printers are now present in 61% of NZ secondary schools (2023 NZCER data) but are predominantly used for curriculum modelling tasks rather than assistive applications.

Opportunity: to develop an open-source, parametric prosthetic hand-attachment library (e-NABLE compatible) sized for 8–18-year-olds, making bespoke assistive devices accessible to schools without specialist fabrication equipment.

junior: Issue: students are spending more time on screens and many teachers report declining reading engagement.
Opportunity: to design a printed reading journal that gives students a structured, screen-free way to track their reading and respond to what they read.
senior: Issue: Ministry of Education data (2023) shows reading-for-pleasure rates among Year 9–10 students declining 18% over five years; teacher interviews identify lack of a structured analog response tool as a contributing factor.

Opportunity: to develop a designed reading journal that scaffolds literary response skills in a deliberate device-free format — addressing both engagement decline and the growing educator demand for screen-free learning tools.

junior: Issue: people who have low vision or limited movement in their hands find it difficult to follow recipe videos on a screen while cooking.
Opportunity: to build a voice-controlled recipe assistant that lets users navigate recipes hands-free, without needing to look at a screen.
senior: Issue: smart-speaker penetration reached 34% of NZ households by 2024 (Statista), yet no dedicated NZ-localised voice-first recipe assistant exists for users with low vision or upper-limb motor impairments.

Opportunity: to develop a voice-first recipe assistant that removes screen dependency entirely — realising the accessibility potential of existing smart-speaker infrastructure for an underserved user group.

junior: Use a sensor to reduce unnecessary watering.
senior: Investigate whether low-cost sensing offers a useful improvement over the existing manual process.

def.junior: Anyone who is affected by or has an interest in your technological outcome. Key stakeholders are directly involved in or directly affected by the outcome or process. Wider stakeholders are less directly affected, but still have some level of interest or influence — or may be impacted in the future.
def.senior: Any individual or group with a vested interest in a technological development or technological outcome. Key stakeholders are those directly influential in, or directly impacted by, the technological practice itself and/or its resulting outcomes (including the technological outcome and any by-products). Wider community stakeholders are less directly influential or impacted, but can be identified as having some level of influence — often through others — and/or may be affected by the project or its outcome in the future.

def.junior: Processes that change materials, energy or information to produce a desired outcome.
def.senior: Controlled changes that turn inputs into outputs. Depending on the discipline and process, material transformations may alter form, structure, composition or performance; energy and information can also be transformed.

junior: Whisking egg whites turns them from liquid into a stiff foam — they are still egg white, but the structure has completely changed.
senior: Mechanical denaturation: whisking egg albumen incorporates air and unfolds globular proteins, creating a semi-stable foam network.
Composition (ovalbumin, ovotransferrin, water) is unchanged; rheological properties (viscosity, yield stress) are transformed.

junior: Felting wool fibres by rubbing them with hot water and soap turns them into a solid, dense fabric — the wool is the same, but it can no longer be pulled apart into separate fibres.
senior: Wet felting: heat, moisture, and friction cause directional scale interlock between keratin fibres, consolidating loose fibre into a non-woven web.
Fibre composition (keratin) is unchanged; tensile, porosity, and drape properties are fundamentally transformed.

junior: Heating and quickly cooling steel (quenching) makes it much harder — it is still steel, but the inside structure has changed.
senior: Quench hardening: rapid cooling from ≥723 °C transforms face-centred cubic austenite to body-centred tetragonal martensite, increasing hardness (up to 65 HRC).
Chemical composition unchanged; subsequent tempering modifies brittleness by partial martensite decomposition.

junior: Converting a vector logo into a JPEG for a website changes it from a set of lines and shapes described by mathematics into a grid of coloured pixels — it looks the same but works very differently.
senior: Rasterisation: vector paths (Bézier curves) are sampled to a pixel grid at a specified resolution.
Visual appearance is preserved within raster constraints; underlying data representation changes from parametric to discrete — scaling behaviour and editability are fundamentally altered.

junior: Compressing a photo from PNG to WebP makes the file much smaller so it loads faster on a website — the image looks almost the same, but the data inside has been reorganised.
senior: Lossy/lossless WebP encoding applies discrete cosine transform (DCT) and entropy coding to pixel data, reducing file size by 25–35% relative to PNG.
Visual content is perceptually preserved; binary structure, colour depth representation, and decoding pathway are transformed.

junior: A motor transforms electrical energy into movement.
senior: Trace energy and information through the system and account for losses and unintended outputs.

def.junior: How easy it is for people to use your outcome to do what it was designed to do. A usable outcome is easy to learn, easy to remember how to use, and leaves people feeling confident.
def.senior: The ease with which people can employ a particular tool or object to achieve a particular goal. Includes learnability, retainability, and user satisfaction. In human-computer interaction, usually refers to the elegance and clarity of a user interface.

junior: A good recipe card has high usability if a Year 7 student who has never cooked before can follow it without asking for help.
senior: A meal-kit package has high usability if a first-time user achieves task completion on first attempt, with a SUS score ≥80 and zero critical navigation errors in think-aloud testing.

junior: A sewing pattern has high usability if a beginner can cut and assemble the garment correctly using only the printed instructions, without needing help.
senior: A pattern has high usability if novice dressmakers achieve task completion on first use, with learnability measured by time-on-task and error count, and retainability assessed at a 2-week retest interval.

junior: A folding bike has high usability if a new user can fold it in under 20 seconds after one demonstration, without looking at the instructions.
senior: A folding bike has high usability if task completion (fold/unfold cycle) is achieved in ≤20 s after a single 30-second demonstration, error-free, with SUS score ≥85 and retention confirmed at a 1-week interval.

junior: A form has high usability if most people can fill it in correctly without needing to re-read anything or ask for help.
senior: A form has high usability if ≥95% of representative users complete it with ≤1 error, mean time-on-task is within 20% of expert benchmark, and post-task confidence is rated ≥4/5 on a Likert scale.

junior: A banking app has high usability if a new user can transfer money to someone else within a few minutes of using it for the first time, without making mistakes.
senior: A banking app has high usability if first-time users achieve ≥95% task completion on the transfer critical path in ≤2 min, with ≤1 navigation error, SUS ≥80, and ≥70% rating the experience as confidence-inspiring post-test.

junior: Make the controls easy to understand.
senior: Test control labels, alert visibility and recovery from mistakes with representative users.

def.junior: Observing representative people completing tasks with an outcome to learn where it supports them or causes difficulty.
def.senior: A planned investigation of representative users performing relevant tasks with a model, prototype or working outcome. junior: Tools used: observation sheet, stopwatch, tally sheet for errors or confusion moments.
Watch five students use the new self-serve salad bar and write down every time they cannot find what they are looking for.
senior: Tools used: think-aloud protocol guide, observation log, stopwatch, video recording (with consent), post-task questionnaire.
Moderated think-aloud study (n=5, Year 7 students): participants verbalise while locating allergen information and serving a meal.
Record task-completion rate, time-on-task, and verbal confusion cues. Results inform label placement revision.

junior: Tools used: printed observation checklist, timer, written feedback form for the participant.
Ask three people who have never seen your pattern to sew the garment while thinking aloud, and note every time they are unsure what to do next.
senior: Tools used: think-aloud protocol, observer notation sheet, video recording, error log spreadsheet.
Think-aloud protocol with three novice dressmakers: participants verbalise interpretation as they follow the pattern.
Record pause duration, re-read frequency, and assembly errors. Data informs notation revision prior to print.

junior: Tools used: observation sheet, stopwatch, written tally for hesitations and wrong-component picks.
Ask five people to assemble your flat-pack stool while saying out loud what they are thinking, and note every time they pick up the wrong piece or get confused.
senior: Tools used: think-aloud protocol, video recording, assembly error log, SUS questionnaire (post-task).
Moderated assembly study (n=5 non-expert participants): participants think aloud while following assembly instructions.
Record hesitations (>5 s), component misidentifications, and sequence deviations. Error clusters inform instruction redesign.

junior: Tools used: printed observation sheet, stopwatch, distance legibility test (tape measure to mark 3 m and 5 m).
Ask users to find a specific article in your redesigned magazine layout while saying out loud what they are looking at, and time how long it takes.
senior: Tools used: think-aloud protocol, Lookback or Maze for remote sessions, time-on-task log, SUS questionnaire, heat-map tool (e.g. Hotjar for digital layouts).
Think-aloud navigation study (n=5 representative readers): participants verbalise while completing a structured search task.
Record time-on-task, verbalised uncertainty, and hierarchy errors. Results inform labelling and typographic hierarchy revision.

junior: Tools used: paper observation sheet, stopwatch, screen recording app (e.g. Loom), error tally sheet.
Sit with five people while they try to book a doctor's appointment on your new website, and write down every time they get stuck or do something unexpected.
senior: Tools used: Maze or Lookback (moderated sessions), Loom for screen + audio capture, SUS questionnaire, task log spreadsheet, axe DevTools for post-session accessibility check.
Moderated usability study (n=5) on staging environment: participants complete GP booking task while thinking aloud.
Record task-completion rate, time-on-task, error count, and SUS score. Severity-rated findings inform prioritised design revision.

junior: Watch a new user reset the watering system.
senior: Observe users completing setup, normal operation and fault recovery, then use the evidence to refine the interface.
